title: Position, Navigation, and Timing Technologies in the 21st Century — Volumes 1 & 2
editors: Y. T. Jade Morton, Frank van Diggelen, James J. Spilker Jr., Bradford W. Parkinson (eds.), Wiley-IEEE Press, 2021
note: Short study notes written in plain words; not text from the book.

chapters.title: Introduction, Early History, and Assuring PNT
chapters.intro: How GPS was born — and why "knowing where you are" needs more than one source.

sections.title: What PNT means
sections.text: PNT = Position, Navigation, Timing. Satnav gives you 4 numbers: 3 for where you are + 1 for time. The goal is "assured" PNT — combine different sources so you're never lost.

sections.title: Navigation before satellites
sections.text: Polynesians steered by stars, the Chinese used the magnetic compass, sailors measured star angles with sextants. Then came radio beacons. Humans always found clever ways to know where they were.

sections.title: The Sputnik spark
sections.text: 1957: scientists tracking Sputnik's Doppler shift could compute its orbit. Big idea: flip it — if you know the satellite's orbit, the Doppler shift tells you where YOU are.

sections.title: Transit: the first satnav
sections.text: That flipped idea became the US Navy's Transit system. It worked, but slowly: one fix took ~15 minutes of listening to a single satellite.

sections.title: Timation and the race
sections.text: The Navy's Timation put precise clocks on satellites. Several competing designs existed until a 1973 meeting merged the best ideas into one plan — GPS.

sections.title: GPS gets the green light
sections.text: December 1973: after weeks of presentations at the Pentagon, the GPS concept was approved almost unchanged. Real building could begin.

sections.title: Three ideas that made GPS work
sections.text: 1) All satellites share one frequency using different codes (CDMA). 2) Ultra-stable atomic clocks in space. 3) Passive users — your receiver only listens. Every GNSS since copied these.

sections.title: Building it for real
sections.text: The team had to predict orbits accurately, make satellites last for years, and build receivers for every kind of user — on a tight, often threatened budget.

chapters.title: Fundamentals of Satellite-Based Navigation and Timing
chapters.intro: The core idea behind every GNSS, explained once.

sections.title: Many ways to locate things
sections.text: Satellites can locate things actively (you transmit) or passively (you only listen). GNSS is passive: billions of receivers, none of them sending anything.

sections.title: Trilateration in one minute
sections.text: Your receiver measures the travel time of signals from satellites → distances. Its own clock is wrong, so we call them "pseudoranges" and use a 4th satellite to solve for that clock error.

sections.title: The space segment
sections.text: Satellites carry atomic clocks and signal generators and fly in a carefully designed constellation, so you always see at least 4 of them.

sections.title: What the signals look like
sections.text: GNSS signals are part radar (precise timing) and part radio (carry data). Spread-spectrum codes let many satellites share the same frequency and resist interference.

sections.title: The ground segment: the brains
sections.text: Monitor stations listen to every satellite, a control center computes orbits and clock errors, and antennas upload fresh corrections to the satellites.

sections.title: Your receiver
sections.text: Antenna → front end → digital tracking → position/velocity/time. Other sensors like inertial units or better clocks can help it when signals are weak.

sections.title: Augmentation
sections.text: Extra help on top of the satellites: phone networks sending assistance data (A-GNSS), correction services, or inertial sensors that keep tracking alive.

sections.title: Where errors come from
sections.text: Four sources: ground segment, satellites (orbit and clock errors), the atmosphere slowing the signal, and your receiver (noise, multipath).

sections.title: DOP: geometry matters
sections.text: Accuracy ≈ ranging error × DOP. Satellites spread across the sky = small DOP = good fix. Height is usually worse than horizontal because no satellites are below you.

chapters.title: The Navstar Global Positioning System
chapters.intro: GPS itself: history, structure, satellites and signals.

sections.title: GPS history in short
sections.text: Tested 1974–85. After Korean Air 007 was shot down in 1983, the US promised free civil GPS. Fully operational in the mid-90s and still being modernized.

sections.title: Who runs GPS
sections.text: A US national executive committee co-chaired by Defense and Transportation sets policy. The US Space Force operates the system.

sections.title: Reference frame and time
sections.text: GPS positions use WGS 84, which is nearly the same as ITRF. GPS time started on 6 Jan 1980, has no leap seconds, and was 18 s ahead of UTC in 2017.

sections.title: The constellation
sections.text: The baseline is 24 slots in 6 orbital planes, about 20,200 km up. In practice ~31 satellites fly for extra coverage.

sections.title: The ground segment
sections.text: A master control station in Colorado with a backup in California, 15+ monitor stations, and ground antennas worldwide uploading corrections.

sections.title: GPS signals
sections.text: Three civil frequencies: L1, L2, L5. Modern civil signals are L1C, L2C and L5, plus military ones. The broadcast "Klobuchar" model removes about half the ionosphere delay.

sections.title: Hidden extra payloads
sections.text: GPS satellites also carry sensors that detect nuclear explosions — a secondary mission since 1980.

sections.title: GPS in one line
sections.text: The first global satnav, used by billions, now being modernized with new satellites, signals and ground control — and increasingly used together with other GNSS.

chapters.title: GLONASS
chapters.intro: Russia's global navigation system.

sections.title: Origins
sections.text: The USSR started with the Doppler-based Cicada system (slow, ~100 m). It then moved to a GPS-like ranging design: GLONASS, first launched in 1982.

sections.title: Its own frame and time
sections.text: GLONASS uses the PZ-90.11 frame and a system time tied to Moscow UTC (UTC + 3 h).

sections.title: Services
sections.text: An open service for everyone and an authorized one for the military. A precise-positioning (PPP) service is coming.

sections.title: The constellation
sections.text: 24 satellites in 3 planes at ~19,100 km — slightly lower than GPS — giving good coverage at high latitudes like Russia.

sections.title: Ground control
sections.text: A control center, central synchronizers built on hydrogen masers, measurement stations, and laser ranging to check the satellites' orbits.

sections.title: Signals: FDMA → CDMA
sections.text: Classic GLONASS gives each satellite its own frequency (FDMA). Newer satellites add GPS-style CDMA signals such as L3OC, which makes mixing with GPS easier.

sections.title: More than navigation
sections.text: Newer GLONASS satellites also relay distress beacons for COSPAS-SARSAT search and rescue.

chapters.title: Galileo
chapters.intro: Europe's civil-controlled GNSS.

sections.title: Why Europe built Galileo
sections.text: To have an independent, civil-controlled system. EGNOS came first as a stepping stone. Galileo carries passive hydrogen masers — among the best clocks ever flown.

sections.title: Who runs it
sections.text: Galileo belongs to the EU. The European Commission manages the program, ESA designs and buys it, and EUSPA runs services. A 2004 EU–US deal made GPS and Galileo work together.

sections.title: Reference frame and time
sections.text: Galileo System Time (GST) and its terrestrial frame are kept within centimetres and nanoseconds of the international standards (ITRF, UTC).

sections.title: Services
sections.text: Open Service (free), High Accuracy Service, PRS (encrypted, government only), and Search & Rescue that confirms to the person in distress that help is coming.

sections.title: Satellites and launches
sections.text: Launched by Soyuz and Ariane from French Guiana. 24 operating satellites plus spares in 3 planes at ~23,200 km.

sections.title: Ground segment
sections.text: Two halves: one controls the satellites, the other computes orbits and clocks every 10 minutes and uploads the navigation message.

sections.title: Signals
sections.text: E1, E5a, E5b, E6. E1 shares the MBOC modulation with GPS L1C, and E5a sits on the same frequency as GPS L5 — so receivers can easily combine them.

sections.title: Ionosphere model
sections.text: Galileo broadcasts NeQuick-G, a model of the ionosphere that single-frequency users apply to correct the signal delay.

sections.title: How accurate
sections.text: The error budget is satellite orbit/clock + atmosphere + receiver. Dual-frequency open-service users get roughly metre-level accuracy.

sections.title: Galileo's future
sections.text: A second generation of Galileo satellites is planned, with better clocks, more flexible signals and more services — and measured accuracy is already better than promised.

chapters.title: BeiDou Navigation Satellite System
chapters.intro: China's GNSS — built in three steps, from regional to global.

sections.title: What makes BeiDou unique
sections.text: "BeiDou" = the Big Dipper. It mixes three orbit types (GEO, IGSO, MEO). Besides positioning it also offers short messaging, augmentation and search & rescue.

sections.title: Three-step plan
sections.text: Step 1: an experimental two-way system (2000). Step 2: a regional system covering Asia-Pacific (2012). Step 3: a global system (around 2020). From regional to global, from active to passive.

sections.title: Frame and time
sections.text: Positions use BDCS/CGCS2000, which is aligned with ITRF. BeiDou Time started on 1 Jan 2006 with no leap seconds and stays within 50 ns of UTC.

sections.title: BDS-I: you had to talk back
sections.text: The first BeiDou was active: your device transmitted to the satellite, and the ground centre computed your position. Bonus: you could send 120-character text messages.

sections.title: BDS-II: regional, GPS-like
sections.text: One-way ranging like GPS, with 14 satellites covering China and Asia-Pacific (2012), while keeping the messaging service.

sections.title: BDS-III: global
sections.text: About 30 satellites. New signals B1C and B2a share frequencies with GPS and Galileo, so multi-GNSS receivers can combine them easily.

sections.title: Smarter messages
sections.text: New navigation messages use strong error-correcting codes (LDPC), so data still gets through when the signal is weak.

chapters.title: IRNSS / NavIC
chapters.intro: India's own regional navigation system.

sections.title: Why India built it
sections.text: During the 1999 Kargil war, India depended on GPS that a foreign country controlled. Answer: NavIC — positioning over India and 1500 km around it.

sections.title: Frame and time
sections.text: NavIC positions use WGS-84. Its system time started on 22 Aug 1999, kept in step with UTC like GPS time.

sections.title: Satellites always overhead
sections.text: Only 7 satellites, but all on geostationary and geosynchronous orbits — so all of them are visible from India all the time.

sections.title: Ground segment
sections.text: Ranging and monitoring stations across India estimate orbits and clocks, with an Indian time centre as the reference.

sections.title: Two bands: L5 and S
sections.text: NavIC transmits on L5 and on the S band (~2.5 GHz) — an unusual choice that also helps correct the ionosphere. There's an open service and a restricted one.

sections.title: Signal guarantees
sections.text: At least −159 dBW on L5 at the ground. Signals are right-hand circularly polarised, like all GNSS.

sections.title: Building a NavIC receiver
sections.text: The antenna must cover L5 and S band. Good receivers combine NavIC with GPS and others for the best availability.

sections.title: Why it matters
sections.text: India owns a constellation that keeps working in a crisis — and it's a great test bed for receiver research.

chapters.title: Quasi-Zenith Satellite System (QZSS)
chapters.intro: Japan's "satellite straight overhead" system.

sections.title: Why Japan needed it
sections.text: Japan is mountains and tall cities: buildings block low satellites. A satellite almost straight overhead (quasi-zenith) solves that, using a figure-8 orbit.

sections.title: Who runs it
sections.text: The Cabinet Office leads it. A private company runs operations from 2018 to 2033 under a public-private finance deal.

sections.title: Same time as GPS
sections.text: QZSS uses GPS's time scale and an ITRF-aligned frame, so receivers treat QZSS satellites almost like extra GPS satellites.

sections.title: Services
sections.text: Extra GPS-like signals, the SLAS (sub-metre) and CLAS (centimetre) correction services, and disaster messages.

sections.title: Constellation
sections.text: Four satellites since 2018 (three on figure-8 orbits, one geostationary), growing to seven so Japan can position without other systems.

sections.title: Ground segment
sections.text: Two control centres 500+ km apart in case of an earthquake, plus tracking stations and 25 monitor stations.

sections.title: Signals
sections.text: L1C/A, L1C, L2C and L5 match GPS. L6 carries centimetre-level corrections, and L1S carries augmentation and disaster alerts.

sections.title: Summary
sections.text: Operational since November 2018, QZSS makes GNSS work better in East Asia and Oceania.

chapters.title: GNSS Interoperability
chapters.intro: How GPS, Galileo, BeiDou and the others work together.

sections.title: What interoperability means
sections.text: Using signals from several systems together to get a better result than any one alone. Coordinated through the UN's International Committee on GNSS (ICG).

sections.title: The ingredients
sections.text: Same centre frequency, similar waveforms, common time and coordinate references. Many satellites = a good fix even in city canyons.

sections.title: GLONASS goes CDMA
sections.text: Old GLONASS gives each satellite its own frequency (FDMA). That causes biases in receivers, so new GLONASS signals use CDMA like everyone else.

sections.title: Why a shared frequency helps
sections.text: Signals on the same frequency pass through the same filters with the same delay, so you don't need to calibrate between them.

sections.title: Different waveforms still work
sections.text: GPS C/A (BPSK) and the modern MBOC signals look different but can be tracked together with standard correlators.

sections.title: Time and coordinate offsets
sections.text: Each system has its own time and frame. Tiny offsets matter to scientists, while phones mostly struggle with multipath and blocked signals.

sections.title: Differential corrections fix it
sections.text: Correction services like WAAS or commercial ones put every system on one common reference, which removes most offset problems.

chapters.title: GNSS Signal Quality Monitoring
chapters.intro: Checking that what satellites transmit is actually healthy.

sections.title: Why we monitor
sections.text: At first, all that mattered was getting a position. Once GPS was operational, providers had to guarantee performance — and that means watching every signal all the time.

sections.title: Who needs it
sections.text: Providers (to prove their service guarantees), safety users like aviation, and high-accuracy networks — they all rely on signals behaving exactly as documented.

sections.title: What to check
sections.text: Power levels, code shape, code–carrier consistency, timing between signals… The GPS civil monitoring specification lists 136 signal requirements.

sections.title: Who's watching today
sections.text: System operators monitor their own satellites. Aviation augmentation systems and the IGS add independent eyes on the ground.

sections.title: How monitors work
sections.text: Track signals with several correlator taps and look at the shape of the correlation peak. A "deformed" peak = a distorted signal that could mislead receivers.

sections.title: What's next
sections.text: More constellations and signals → standards and monitors need to keep up, especially for aviation and other safety uses.

chapters.title: GNSS Orbit Determination and Time Synchronization
chapters.intro: How we know exactly where each satellite is and what its clock says.

sections.title: What's measured
sections.text: Ground stations record code and carrier-phase measurements. The model includes clocks, biases, ionosphere, troposphere, antenna offsets and relativity.

sections.title: What moves a satellite
sections.text: Earth's lumpy gravity, Sun and Moon, solar radiation pressure, plus relativity (GPS clocks are tuned to run slightly slow before launch).

sections.title: Solving for orbits
sections.text: Least squares or Kalman filters estimate orbits and clocks together. Satellite manoeuvres are tricky because outsiders don't know when they happen.

sections.title: Products you can use
sections.text: Broadcast orbits (~1 m) come from the control segment. IGS precise orbits reach the centimetre level — for science and PPP.

chapters.title: Ground-Based Augmentation System (GBAS)
chapters.intro: GNSS-based precision landing at airports.

sections.title: What GBAS is
sections.text: A local differential GNSS station at an airport. It sends corrections and integrity data over VHF so aircraft know their position to about 1 m.

sections.title: Why replace ILS?
sections.text: ILS (the classic landing system) needs one installation per runway end, is sensitive to terrain, and can't do curved approaches. One GBAS can serve the whole airport.

sections.title: History
sections.text: 1990s FAA trials made 400+ automatic landings using differential GPS. That led to LAAS, now called GBAS.

sections.title: Performance levels
sections.text: Landing categories I, II and III set how low a pilot can go before seeing the runway. GBAS service types GAST C and GAST D aim to match them.

sections.title: What gets broadcast
sections.text: Corrections twice per second plus integrity parameters. With them the aircraft gets about 1 m accuracy.

sections.title: Integrity monitors
sections.text: Many checks on the ground — signal quality, data quality, consistency between reference receivers — catch faults before they reach the aircraft.

sections.title: Proving it's safe (CAT I)
sections.text: Protection levels must stay below alert limits even if a satellite or reference receiver fails.

sections.title: Going further (CAT III)
sections.text: Stricter rules: catch faults within 1.5 s and keep the risk of an undetected error >1.8 m below one in a billion.

sections.title: Where it is today
sections.text: About 30 airports worldwide. Major airlines fly GBAS approaches. Dual-frequency and multi-constellation versions are coming.

chapters.title: Satellite-Based Augmentation Systems (SBAS)
chapters.intro: WAAS, EGNOS, GAGAN & co: corrections and integrity from geostationary satellites.

sections.title: What SBAS does
sections.text: Ground networks monitor GNSS and send corrections plus "trust bounds" through geostationary satellites. If something goes wrong, pilots are warned within 6 seconds.

sections.title: Threats
sections.text: Clock, orbit, ionosphere and other errors — some hit one satellite, some hit all. Threat models say how big and how likely each one is.

sections.title: Integrity monitors
sections.text: WAAS uses 38 reference stations. It sends error bounds for each satellite (UDRE) and for the ionosphere (GIVE).

sections.title: The message
sections.text: 250-bit messages every second from geostationary satellites: fast and slow corrections, ionosphere grids and integrity information.

sections.title: Systems worldwide
sections.text: WAAS (USA), EGNOS (Europe), MSAS (Japan), GAGAN (India), SDCM (Russia), and plans in Africa and Asia. SBAS can guide aircraft down to about 200 ft.

sections.title: Next generation
sections.text: Dual-frequency, multi-constellation SBAS uses GPS L5 and Galileo E5a to remove most of the ionosphere error.

chapters.title: Fundamentals and Overview of GNSS Receivers
chapters.intro: What's inside the box that turns faint satellite signals into your position.

sections.title: Three blocks
sections.text: Every receiver has an RF front end (antenna signal → digital samples), a baseband processor (finds and tracks signals) and a system processor (computes your position).

sections.title: The oscillator matters
sections.text: The crystal oscillator is the receiver's heartbeat — and its only "moving part". Vibration and temperature shake it, and that limits how weak a signal you can track.

sections.title: The RF front end
sections.text: It amplifies a signal of microvolts by over 100 dB, filters out interference, shifts the frequency down, and digitizes it. Noise figure and linearity are key.

sections.title: Sampling choices
sections.text: Most receivers shift the frequency down before sampling. Sampling the RF directly is becoming possible, but needs fast ADCs and lots of power.

sections.title: Correlation: finding a buried signal
sections.text: GNSS signals sit below the noise. The receiver multiplies the input by a local copy of the code — when they line up, a correlation peak pops out of the noise.

sections.title: Channel states
sections.text: Each channel steps through search → acquire → track → read data, and estimates signal strength (C/N0) as it goes.

sections.title: Timekeeping inside
sections.text: Measurements from all satellites must be taken at the same receiver instant. The receiver's own clock isn't accurate — GNSS corrects it.

sections.title: The future
sections.text: Receivers specialise by application. Flexible, software-programmable chips will likely dominate.

chapters.title: GNSS Receiver Signal Tracking
chapters.intro: How a receiver locks on to code and carrier — and stays locked.

sections.title: What tracking does
sections.text: Continuously estimates the code phase and carrier phase of each signal to get its time of arrival. It also finds data-bit edges so the navigation message can be read.

sections.title: The loop idea
sections.text: Correlate → discriminator measures the error → filter smooths it → oscillator (NCO) adjusts the local copy. Repeat about every millisecond.

sections.title: Code tracking (DLL)
sections.text: Early, prompt and late correlators. If early > late, the local code is lagging, so nudge it. Narrower spacing = more precise and less multipath.

sections.title: Carrier tracking (PLL/FLL)
sections.text: A PLL follows carrier phase (most precise, but fragile). An FLL follows only frequency (tougher, but less precise). Carrier tracking is the weak link.

sections.title: Advanced carrier tracking
sections.text: Kalman-filter (state-space) designs adapt to the signal strength, receiver dynamics and oscillator quality — key for cities, forests, scintillation and fast platforms.

sections.title: Takeaway
sections.text: Classic loops work fine in normal conditions. Tougher conditions need optimised designs and help from other sensors.

chapters.title: Vector Processing
chapters.intro: Track all satellites together, not one by one.

sections.title: Scalar vs vector
sections.text: A normal receiver tracks each satellite separately. A vector receiver predicts every signal from one shared position/velocity estimate — so strong satellites help the weak ones.

sections.title: Vector DLL/FLL
sections.text: One central navigation filter drives every channel's code and frequency. More robust at low signal strength and in foliage, but the carrier phase isn't tracked.

sections.title: Hybrid designs
sections.text: Combine vector robustness for code and frequency with classic PLLs for precise carrier phase.

sections.title: Vector phase tracking
sections.text: Tracking carrier phase in vector form keeps centimetre-level phase alive through signal fades and blockages — hard, but powerful.

sections.title: Bottom line
sections.text: Tests with real signals and simulators show vector receivers beat conventional ones in tough conditions.

chapters.title: Assisted GNSS
chapters.intro: How your phone gets a fix in seconds.

sections.title: A-GNSS is about search
sections.text: Yes, A-GNSS sends orbits over the internet. But the real win is shrinking the search for signals — faster first fix AND higher sensitivity.

sections.title: The search space
sections.text: Without help, a receiver must scan every frequency (unknown Doppler and clock offset) and every code delay for every satellite. Like scanning a radio dial in the dark.

sections.title: How assistance shrinks it
sections.text: Know roughly the time, your position and the orbits → predict each satellite's Doppler. The search becomes about 100× smaller.

sections.title: Code-delay help
sections.text: If the assisted time is accurate to microseconds, you can also predict where the code peak sits. A few km of position error barely matters.

sections.title: Satellite speed
sections.text: GNSS satellites move at ~3–4 km/s, but the range to you changes at most ~800 m/s. That sets how big the Doppler uncertainty is.

sections.title: Real numbers
sections.text: For each 1 km of position error, the predicted Doppler is off by only a few Hz — tiny. Time error matters more.

sections.title: Search tables
sections.text: Handy lookup tables give the assisted search-space size for GPS, Galileo, BeiDou and GLONASS on each band.

sections.title: Where assistance comes from
sections.text: Reference networks (IGS or company networks) collect ephemeris, and location servers send it to phones via cellular standards (3GPP, SUPL). Long-term orbits extend it to days.

sections.title: Summary
sections.text: A-GNSS reduces the frequency search by 100×+, makes the first fix fast, and lets the receiver integrate longer for high sensitivity.

chapters.title: High-Sensitivity GNSS
chapters.intro: Getting a fix indoors and inside a tiny phone.

sections.title: Why sensitivity matters
sections.text: Phone antennas are tiny and signals indoors are 100–1000× weaker. Acquisition is the hard part, tracking is easier.

sections.title: Signal → C/N0 → SNR
sections.text: Follow the signal from the antenna through the front end to the correlator peak. Design goal: a tall peak even when the signal is weak.

sections.title: Receiver blocks
sections.text: Satellite: code + data + carrier. Receiver: remove the carrier, multiply by a local code, add up over time. Every design follows that path.

sections.title: Front-end noise
sections.text: The first amplifier (LNA) and any cable loss before it set the noise figure — every dB lost there is lost forever.

sections.title: Coherent integration
sections.text: Adding correlator outputs in phase over longer times raises the SNR. But data bits and frequency error limit how long you can add.

sections.title: Non-coherent integration
sections.text: Add up the magnitude of many short coherent sums. Phase changes no longer cancel the signal — the price is a "squaring loss".

sections.title: How weak can phones go?
sections.text: Phones acquire signals around −150 dBm and reach a practical limit near −156 dBm. Beyond that, search time and oscillator drift win.

sections.title: Simpler future signals?
sections.text: The author's argument: each satellite has limited power. Fewer, simpler, stronger signals might help everyone more than many complex, weaker ones.

chapters.title: Relative Positioning and RTK
chapters.intro: Centimetres by comparing your receiver with a nearby reference station.

sections.title: Why go relative
sections.text: Most devices are happy with metres. Surveying, construction and farming need centimetres — so we difference our measurements against a reference receiver.

sections.title: How differencing works
sections.text: Errors common to both receivers (satellite clock, orbit, most of the atmosphere) cancel when you subtract their measurements. Double differences also remove the receiver clocks.

sections.title: Ambiguity resolution
sections.text: Carrier phase is millimetre-precise, but its whole number of cycles is unknown. Fix those integers correctly and you get centimetre accuracy. RTK does this in real time.

sections.title: Network RTK
sections.text: Single-base RTK works up to ~10–15 km. A network of stations models the atmosphere and orbit errors, so corrections cover whole regions — streamed via RTCM/NTRIP.

sections.title: Today and next
sections.text: Network RTK is the standard for surveying and precision farming. It's now merging with PPP into PPP-RTK.

chapters.title: GNSS Precise Point Positioning (PPP)
chapters.intro: High accuracy anywhere with one receiver.

sections.title: What PPP is
sections.text: Use precise satellite orbits and clocks (from IGS or a service) plus carrier phase on one receiver. Centimetre-to-decimetre accuracy anywhere — no local base station needed.

sections.title: The math in words
sections.text: Model everything: geometry, clocks, hardware biases, ionosphere, troposphere, and the carrier-phase ambiguities, then estimate what's left.

sections.title: Single vs dual frequency
sections.text: With two frequencies you can cancel the ionosphere. Single-frequency PPP must correct or estimate it — cheaper, but less accurate.

sections.title: Beyond positioning
sections.text: The same processing gives water vapour for weather forecasts, ionosphere maps and precise time transfer.

sections.title: Orbit & clock services
sections.text: Post-processed online services (CSRS-PPP, APPS…) and real-time streams over the internet or satellite (IGS RTS, Galileo HAS, commercial services).

sections.title: Corrections you need
sections.text: Antenna phase-centre offsets, relativity, phase wind-up, Earth tides and ocean loading — skip them and you lose centimetres.

sections.title: PPP-RTK
sections.text: PPP's weakness is slow convergence (tens of minutes). Send satellite phase biases as well, and the integer ambiguities can be fixed — accuracy in minutes.

sections.title: Multi-frequency
sections.text: Three or more frequencies make ambiguities easier to fix. Adding regional ionosphere corrections cut convergence from ~40 min to under 5 min in the book's example.

sections.title: Multi-GNSS
sections.text: More satellites → faster convergence and more robustness. Remember to handle the inter-system biases between constellations.

chapters.title: Direct Position Estimation (DPE)
chapters.intro: Skip the pseudoranges — go straight from raw signal to position.

sections.title: One step instead of two
sections.text: A normal receiver measures ranges, then solves for position. DPE tests candidate positions directly against the raw signal from all satellites at once.

sections.title: Conventional pipeline
sections.text: Signal model → correlate → pseudoranges → least squares. DPE reuses the same building blocks, just in a different order.

sections.title: Making it practical
sections.text: Searching a grid of positions is heavy. FFT-based correlation and parallel computing make it feasible.

sections.title: Variants
sections.text: Duty-cycled DPE (receiver on only 2% of the time) saves power. Direct Time Estimation serves timing users with known positions.

sections.title: Verdict
sections.text: More accurate and robust in cities and with weak signals, at the cost of computing power — getting cheaper every year.

chapters.title: Multipath and NLOS
chapters.intro: The main error source in cities — reflected signals.

sections.title: Two different problems
sections.text: NLOS: you only receive a reflection → always a positive range error. Multipath: direct + reflected mixed → positive or negative error, depending on receiver design.

sections.title: How reflections behave
sections.text: Smooth surfaces give strong mirror-like reflections that flip polarisation (RHCP → LHCP). Rough surfaces scatter. Low-elevation satellites get hit most.

sections.title: Receiver-side fixes
sections.text: Choke-ring antennas, narrow and multipath-mitigating correlators, and polarisation tricks reduce multipath before measurements are formed.

sections.title: Carrier smoothing
sections.text: Blend noisy-but-absolute code with smooth-but-ambiguous carrier phase (Hatch filter) → cleaner pseudoranges.

sections.title: Navigation-level fixes
sections.text: De-weight low-C/N0 satellites, run consistency checks, use 3D city maps ("shadow matching") to spot and even exploit blocked signals.

sections.title: Post-processing tricks
sections.text: Satellite geometry repeats (GPS every sidereal day), so multipath at a fixed site repeats too — measure it one day and subtract it the next (sidereal filtering).

sections.title: Summary
sections.text: Multipath is often the dominant error. Phones are the hardest case. Better maps, sensors and computing keep improving things.

chapters.title: GNSS Integrity and RAIM
chapters.intro: How much can you trust your position?

sections.title: What integrity is
sections.text: Accuracy = typical error. Integrity = trust: knowing with tiny risk (like 1 in 10 million) that the error is below a bound — and getting warned in time if it isn't.

sections.title: The four requirements
sections.text: Accuracy, integrity, continuity (don't drop out mid-operation) and availability. Tighter integrity can cost continuity and availability.

sections.title: Risk as a chain
sections.text: Risk = chance a fault exists × chance the monitor misses it × chance the error then exceeds the bound. Add it up over all fault types.

sections.title: Protection levels
sections.text: The receiver computes in real time a bound it guarantees the error stays within. Is it smaller than the alert limit? Then the operation is available.

sections.title: Bounding the unknown
sections.text: Real error distributions have heavy tails we can't fully measure. So we "overbound" them with safely conservative Gaussians.

sections.title: Threat models
sections.text: Each possible fault (satellite clock jump, bad orbit, ionosphere storm) gets a simplified model with bounded size and probability.

sections.title: RAIM
sections.text: Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring: with more satellites than needed, the receiver checks whether they agree. A disagreement points to a faulty one.

sections.title: Advanced RAIM (ARAIM)
sections.text: Dual-frequency, multi-constellation RAIM. Lots of redundant, ionosphere-free measurements could let aircraft use RAIM even for vertical guidance.

sections.title: Summary
sections.text: Integrity and continuity pull in opposite directions. Meeting both at aviation-level probabilities takes careful, conservative design.

chapters.title: Interference: Origins, Effects, and Mitigation
chapters.intro: Jamming — and why GNSS is a "stealth utility".

sections.title: The stealth utility
sections.text: GNSS is hidden inside phone networks, power grids, ships and hospitals. When it's jammed, strange things fail — dropped calls, lost radar positions, broken pagers.

sections.title: Ways to attack
sections.text: Jamming (noise that drowns the signal), data spoofing (fake corrections or ephemeris), and RF overlays (full fake GNSS signals).

sections.title: How far jamming reaches
sections.text: GNSS signals are about −160 dBW. A cheap jammer of a fraction of a watt can blind receivers for hundreds of metres to kilometres.

sections.title: Old signal weaknesses
sections.text: GPS L1 C/A has short codes with spectral lines, so a tone at the wrong frequency hurts it a lot. Modern signals are much more robust.

sections.title: Mitigation
sections.text: Better signals, notch filters, antenna arrays that null the jammer, and IMU aiding. Most civil "PPDs" (personal privacy devices) are crude.

sections.title: Situational awareness
sections.text: Receivers can measure the noise floor and recognise jamming types (pulse, CW, wideband) — like a smoke alarm: it doesn't stop the fire, but you know.

sections.title: Authenticated signals
sections.text: Cryptographic signatures or encrypted codes (like Galileo OSNMA) make faking signals much harder.

sections.title: Proof of location
sections.text: Location is part of identity for banks, power grids and remote devices — so being able to prove where you are matters.

sections.title: Closing
sections.text: Even military encryption depends on trusting thousands of keyed devices. There's no single silver bullet; layers of defence work best.

chapters.title: Civilian GNSS Spoofing, Detection, and Recovery
chapters.intro: Fake satellites — and how receivers fight back.

sections.title: What spoofing is
sections.text: Broadcasting false GNSS signals to mislead a receiver. Civil codes are public, so they're easy to imitate. Demonstrated since 2003, now seen in the wild.

sections.title: Attack methods
sections.text: From simple fake-signal generators, to meaconing (record & replay), to "drag-off" attacks that slowly pull your position away, to software-only attacks on the receiver.

sections.title: Detection
sections.text: Watch for oddities: signals all arriving from one direction, suspicious power levels, distorted correlation peaks, clashes with IMU/clock, or missing authentication.

sections.title: Recovery
sections.text: Detect → find the authentic signals hidden under the fakes → verify them → navigate on them again. Knowing you're lost beats trusting a fake fix.

sections.title: Testing defences
sections.text: Defences need realistic testing with spoofing simulators and live-sky trials, under realistic power advantages.

chapters.title: GNSS Receiver Antennas and Antenna Arrays
chapters.intro: The antenna shapes everything the receiver sees.

sections.title: Antenna basics
sections.text: Active antennas have a built-in LNA so long cables don't kill the signal. Key specs: gain pattern, polarisation (RHCP), bandwidth and phase centre.

sections.title: Antennas aren't points
sections.text: The real "phase centre" moves with direction and frequency, adding millimetre-to-centimetre biases — that's why calibration (ANTEX) matters for precise work.

sections.title: Common types
sections.text: Patch antennas (cheap, flat), helix, and choke-ring designs (big, great at blocking multipath) for reference stations.

sections.title: Antenna arrays
sections.text: Several elements together can steer beams towards satellites or switch patterns — useful on aircraft and vehicles.

sections.title: Array processing
sections.text: Combine element outputs digitally to place nulls on jammers and beams on satellites — the strongest defence against interference.

sections.title: Summary
sections.text: Smaller devices, more signals, higher precision — the antenna is often the deciding factor. Don't treat it as an afterthought.

chapters.title: Global Geodesy and Reference Frames
chapters.intro: Measuring a moving Earth — and agreeing on coordinates.

sections.title: What geodesy is
sections.text: The science of Earth's shape, gravity and rotation. All three change: plates drift, ice melts, water moves. Space techniques (GNSS, VLBI, SLR) measure them to millimetres.

sections.title: The IGS
sections.text: The International GNSS Service: 400+ volunteer-run stations worldwide sharing data, producing precise orbits, clocks and station positions — free for everyone.

sections.title: Reference frames (ITRF)
sections.text: A coordinate system needs a physical realisation: station positions AND velocities. ITRF combines GNSS, VLBI, SLR and DORIS, and is the backbone for WGS 84, GTRF and the others.

chapters.title: GNSS Geodesy in Geophysics, Hazards, Climate, and Environment
chapters.intro: Using millimetre GNSS to watch the planet.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: Permanent GNSS stations measure ground motion continuously — from slow plate drift to earthquake shaking.

sections.title: Geodetic-quality GPS
sections.text: Choke-ring antennas, stable monuments and careful processing give millimetre-level daily positions.

sections.title: Tectonics
sections.text: GNSS velocities show plates moving a few cm per year and strain building up on faults — the slow lead-up to earthquakes.

sections.title: Natural hazards
sections.text: High-rate GNSS measures earthquake displacement in real time, helping rapid magnitude estimates and tsunami warnings. It also tracks volcanoes and landslides.

sections.title: Climate
sections.text: GNSS tracks sea-level change (correcting tide gauges for land motion), ice loss via the ground rebounding, and water vapour in the atmosphere.

sections.title: Environment
sections.text: Reflected signals at stations measure snow depth, soil moisture, vegetation and water levels, and loading shows groundwater changes.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.text: Dense GNSS networks have become a core instrument for Earth science and hazard response.

chapters.title: Distributing Time and Frequency Information
chapters.intro: How the world shares one precise clock.

sections.title: Clocks and statistics
sections.text: Every clock drifts. The Allan variance describes how stable a clock is over different averaging times.

sections.title: Accuracy and traceability
sections.text: Your time is only as good as the chain linking it back to UTC via national labs.

sections.title: Measuring delays (one-way)
sections.text: To transfer time, you must know the signal delay — GNSS common-view and all-in-view compare clocks across continents.

sections.title: Measuring delays (two-way)
sections.text: Two-way methods (satellite or fibre) cancel most of the path delay because the signal travels both ways.

sections.title: Synchronisation strategies
sections.text: Choose by need: NTP over the internet (milliseconds), PTP on networks (microseconds or better), GNSS (nanoseconds).

sections.title: Real data
sections.text: Examples compare methods and show the noise and drift each one really has.

sections.title: Steering clocks
sections.text: Control algorithms gently steer a local clock towards a reference without causing jumps.

sections.title: Summary
sections.text: Precise time underpins power grids, telecoms and finance — and GNSS is the most widely used way to deliver it.

chapters.title: GNSS for Neutral Atmosphere and Severe Weather
chapters.intro: Water vapour from GNSS delays.

sections.title: Tropospheric delay
sections.text: The lower atmosphere delays signals by ~2.4 m at zenith. The "wet" part depends on water vapour — so GNSS can measure it.

sections.title: Water vapour monitoring
sections.text: Zenith wet delay converts to precipitable water vapour. Networks give continuous, all-weather humidity maps, and tomography gives 3D structure.

sections.title: Case studies
sections.text: GNSS water vapour shows the moisture build-up before thunderstorms and heavy rain, and improves forecasts.

sections.title: Applications
sections.text: Weather services feed GNSS data into forecasts every day. Real-time PPP and denser networks extend it further.

chapters.title: Ionospheric Effects, Monitoring, and Mitigation
chapters.intro: The charged upper atmosphere and what it does to signals.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: The ionosphere (60–1000 km) is ionised by the Sun. It's the largest error source for single-frequency users and a playground for space-weather science.

sections.title: Ionosphere basics
sections.text: Electron density changes with time of day, season, solar cycle, latitude and storms. TEC (total electron content) sums it along the signal path.

sections.title: Refraction effects
sections.text: The ionosphere delays code and advances carrier phase — by an amount proportional to TEC/f². Dual-frequency users cancel most of it, and single-frequency users use models.

sections.title: Scintillation
sections.text: Small-scale irregularities make signals flicker in amplitude and phase, mostly near the equator and poles — causing cycle slips and loss of lock.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.text: Robust tracking, multi-frequency signals and monitoring networks help — and GNSS itself is a great ionosphere sensor.

chapters.title: GNSS for Detecting Natural and Man-Made Hazards
chapters.intro: The ionosphere as an alarm bell.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: Earthquakes, tsunamis, volcanoes and even explosions shake the atmosphere. The waves travel up and leave fingerprints in GNSS TEC.

sections.title: Ionospheric observables
sections.text: Filtered TEC from dense GNSS networks reveals travelling disturbances from below.

sections.title: Earthquakes and tsunamis
sections.text: Big earthquakes push air upward and the signature reaches the ionosphere within ~10 min. Tsunamis create gravity waves that GNSS can see over the open ocean.

sections.title: Volcanic eruptions
sections.text: Explosive eruptions send acoustic waves into the ionosphere, visible in TEC.

sections.title: Thunderstorms
sections.text: Strong convective storms create atmospheric gravity waves seen as ripples in TEC.

sections.title: Asteroids and meteors
sections.text: Large bolides exploding in the atmosphere leave detectable ionospheric signatures.

sections.title: From space
sections.text: GNSS receivers on satellites (radio occultation) add views of disturbances from orbit.

sections.title: Combining ground and space
sections.text: Merging ground networks with space observations gives a fuller 3D picture.

sections.title: Coupled models
sections.text: Models linking ocean, atmosphere and ionosphere predict what a tsunami's signal should look like, so it can be detected.

sections.title: Inversion
sections.text: Working backwards from TEC changes to estimate the source — like the tsunami height.

sections.title: Man-made hazards
sections.text: Rocket launches, underground nuclear tests and large explosions also leave ionospheric fingerprints.

sections.title: Precursors?
sections.text: Claims of pre-earthquake ionospheric signals exist but are still debated.

sections.title: Outlook
sections.text: Real-time GNSS ionospheric monitoring could add minutes to tsunami warnings.

chapters.title: GNSS Radio Occultation
chapters.intro: Profiling the atmosphere from orbit.

sections.title: The idea
sections.text: A low-orbit satellite watches a GNSS satellite set or rise behind Earth's limb. The atmosphere bends the signal — and that bending reveals temperature, pressure and humidity profiles.

sections.title: System design
sections.text: Missions like COSMIC need accurate receivers, good clocks and many occultations per day around the globe.

sections.title: Design considerations
sections.text: Open-loop tracking for the turbulent lower troposphere, precise orbits and antenna design all matter.

sections.title: Science
sections.text: Occultation data is one of the most valuable inputs to weather forecasts and gives a stable, calibration-free climate record. It also profiles the ionosphere.

chapters.title: GNSS Reflectometry (GNSS-R)
chapters.intro: Using reflected GNSS signals as a free radar.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: GNSS signals bounce off oceans, land and ice. Catching the reflections turns every satellite into a free bistatic radar.

sections.title: General characteristics
sections.text: Weak, spread-out reflections from a "glistening zone" around the mirror point. Receivers map them as delay-Doppler maps.

sections.title: Geometry
sections.text: The specular point, its delay and Doppler depend on where the transmitter and receiver are — computed precisely to locate the measurement.

sections.title: Fundamentals
sections.text: Bistatic radar equation, surface roughness and polarisation decide how much power comes back.

sections.title: Reflection models
sections.text: Models of how rough surfaces scatter the signal turn measured waveforms into geophysical values.

sections.title: Ocean winds
sections.text: Rougher sea = more spread reflection → wind speed. NASA's CYGNSS uses this to measure winds inside hurricanes.

sections.title: Ocean altimetry
sections.text: Reflection delay gives sea-surface height — promising for dense coverage, still being refined.

sections.title: Soil moisture
sections.text: Wetter soil reflects more strongly — from space or from ground stations.

sections.title: Snow and ice
sections.text: Reflections measure snow depth, sea-ice extent and thickness hints.

sections.title: Other land variables
sections.text: Vegetation, flooding and wetlands also show up in reflected signals.

sections.title: Summary
sections.text: GNSS-R is a cheap, growing Earth-observation technique using signals that are already everywhere.

chapters.title: Overview of Volume 2: Integrated PNT
chapters.intro: Beyond GNSS — every other way to know where you are.

sections.title: One loop for all navigation
sections.text: Every navigation system does the same thing: predict your state → observe something → compare → correct. GNSS, inertial, cameras, radio — all fit this loop.

sections.title: What Volume 2 covers
sections.text: Signals of opportunity (cell, TV, LEO), inertial sensors and clocks, maps, lasers and cameras, celestial sources, animal navigation, and real applications from farms to the Arctic.

chapters.title: Nonlinear Recursive Estimation
chapters.intro: The math engine of sensor fusion: Kalman filters and beyond.

sections.title: Why Kalman filters rule
sections.text: Since 1960 the Kalman filter has been THE tool for navigation: optimal, recursive and fast enough to run in real time.

sections.title: Linear foundations
sections.text: A state (position, velocity…), a motion model with process noise, and measurements with noise. Predict, then update with a weighted correction.

sections.title: When things aren't linear
sections.text: Real navigation is nonlinear. The extended KF linearises, the unscented KF uses sample points, and particle filters use many weighted guesses — each trading accuracy for compute.

sections.title: Choosing a filter
sections.text: No filter is best everywhere. Hybrids often win — pick based on how nonlinear the problem is and your computing budget.

chapters.title: Indoor Navigation Techniques
chapters.intro: Where GPS can't reach.

sections.title: Why indoors is hard
sections.text: GNSS signals are too weak to get through walls and roofs. Indoor positioning needs other signals and sensors.

sections.title: Key terms
sections.text: Absolute vs relative location, symbolic location ("room 204"), and device-based vs infrastructure-based systems.

sections.title: How to judge a system
sections.text: Accuracy, precision, coverage, latency, cost, power and privacy. Signal strength falls with distance — a rough way to estimate range.

sections.title: Signals used indoors
sections.text: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth beacons, UWB, RFID, ultrasound, infrared, visible light and magnetic fields — each with its own range and accuracy.

sections.title: Techniques
sections.text: Triangulation/trilateration, fingerprinting (matching a signal "map"), proximity, and dead reckoning with phone sensors. Hybrids work best.

sections.title: Open problems
sections.text: Cost of infrastructure, keeping fingerprint maps up to date, device differences and privacy are still unsolved.

chapters.title: Navigation with Cellular Signals of Opportunity
chapters.intro: Using phone towers like GPS satellites.

sections.title: Why cellular signals
sections.text: They're everywhere, 20+ dB stronger than GPS, cover many frequencies and come from many directions — and they're free to listen to.

sections.title: Cellular systems in brief
sections.text: From 1G to 5G: CDMA and LTE broadcast known pilot and sync signals that a receiver can use for ranging.

sections.title: The clock problem
sections.text: Towers aren't perfectly synchronised. Their clock errors must be modelled and estimated as part of navigation.

sections.title: Frameworks
sections.text: Either map tower positions and clocks with a reference receiver, or estimate them on the fly (radio SLAM).

sections.title: CDMA navigation
sections.text: CDMA towers broadcast known codes with timing offsets, so receivers measure pseudoranges much like GPS.

sections.title: LTE navigation
sections.text: LTE sync and reference signals give ranges good to a few metres in tests — in places where GPS struggles.

sections.title: Sector clock mismatch
sections.text: One tower has several sectors that may have slightly different clock biases — something to model.

sections.title: Mixing with GNSS
sections.text: Towers sit near the horizon and fill the geometry gaps GNSS leaves, especially improving vertical accuracy.

sections.title: Cellular-aided INS
sections.text: When GNSS is lost, cellular signals keep inertial drift in check, for kilometres of driving.

chapters.title: Metropolitan Beacon Systems
chapters.intro: Dedicated city beacons for indoor/urban PNT.

sections.title: What MBS is
sections.text: A network of terrestrial beacons broadcasting GPS-like signals in licensed spectrum, built for cities and indoors — for E911 and as a GNSS backup.

sections.title: Why it works
sections.text: Synchronised transmitters on rooftops plus a barometer for height — reaching metre-level positioning and accurate timing where GNSS can't.

chapters.title: Navigation with Digital TV Signals
chapters.intro: Broadcast towers as navigation beacons.

sections.title: PNT from broadcasts
sections.text: TV towers are powerful, fixed and well-known. Their signals carry timing structures you can use to measure ranges.

sections.title: Signal types
sections.text: ATSC (USA), DVB-T (Europe), DTMB (China): each has sync patterns or pilots usable for time of arrival.

sections.title: Pseudoranges
sections.text: Measure arrival times against your own clock. Like GNSS, tower clock offsets must be removed — with a reference receiver or by differencing.

sections.title: Practical issues
sections.text: Multipath in cities, unknown tower clocks and poor geometry (towers are all on the horizon) are the main challenges.

chapters.title: Low-Frequency Radio Navigation (Loran/eLoran)
chapters.intro: A powerful ground-based backup to GNSS.

sections.title: Why we still need it
sections.text: GNSS is weak and shares vulnerabilities. A very different, very strong signal (100 kHz, megawatts) makes a great backup.

sections.title: History
sections.text: From WWII LORAN to Loran-C. It was switched off in the US in 2010 — and since revived interest as eLoran.

sections.title: Signals
sections.text: Pulses at 100 kHz in timed sequences from chains of stations. eLoran adds precise timing and data.

sections.title: What eLoran adds
sections.text: A data channel carrying corrections, integrity warnings and UTC time — enabling ~10 m positioning and ~50 ns timing.

sections.title: Propagation
sections.text: Ground waves follow Earth's surface predictably. Sky waves bounce off the ionosphere and interfere. Land changes the speed (ASF corrections).

sections.title: Noise
sections.text: Atmospheric noise from lightning and man-made interference set limits. Magnetic loop antennas help.

sections.title: Receivers
sections.text: Modern digital eLoran receivers use H-field antennas, track all stations together, and decode the data channel.

sections.title: Performance
sections.text: Loran-C was certified for marine and en-route aviation. eLoran reaches harbour-entrance accuracy.

sections.title: Future
sections.text: Low-frequency systems could also broadcast authenticated data and resilient time for critical infrastructure.

chapters.title: Adaptive Radar Navigation
chapters.intro: Seeing the ground with radio echoes.

sections.title: History
sections.text: Radar was born for detection, but aircraft soon used ground-mapping radar to navigate by recognising terrain and landmarks.

sections.title: Modern radar localisation
sections.text: Digital processing turned radar into a precise navigation sensor that works through clouds, smoke and darkness.

sections.title: Signal processing
sections.text: Wideband signals give fine range resolution, but need heavy computing. Radar sees the world differently from cameras.

sections.title: SAR methods
sections.text: Synthetic aperture radar builds high-resolution images by combining echoes along the flight path. Matching them to maps gives position.

sections.title: UWB-OFDM case study
sections.text: Robust, interference-resistant radar waveforms tracking strong stationary reflectors can navigate without GNSS.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.text: As computing grew, radar went from analog aid to a powerful GNSS-independent navigation sensor.

chapters.title: Navigation from Low Earth Orbit (LEO)
chapters.intro: The new mega-constellations as navigation sources.

sections.title: Three orbit regimes
sections.text: LEO (<2000 km), MEO (where GNSS lives) and GEO. Most satellites now fly in LEO — thousands of them.

sections.title: Why LEO is attractive
sections.text: ~20× closer than GNSS → ~30 dB stronger signals, fast geometry change (great for Doppler and convergence), but smaller footprints and fast passes.

sections.title: LEO navigation today
sections.text: Transit was LEO. Iridium now offers a time and location service (STL), and LEO data can speed up PPP convergence.

sections.title: LEO navigation tomorrow
sections.text: Dedicated LEO-PNT constellations with cheap commercial parts could match or beat GPS, with stronger, jam-resistant signals.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.text: LEO complements GNSS: stronger signals, better geometry dynamics and more resilience.

sections.title: Using broadband LEO as-is
sections.text: Instead of new PNT satellites, exploit existing broadband signals (Starlink, OneWeb, Orbcomm) as signals of opportunity.

sections.title: Measurements
sections.text: Pseudorange, carrier phase and Doppler can be pulled out of LEO signals with a suitable receiver.

sections.title: Orbits
sections.text: LEO orbits are known only roughly (public TLEs). Simple dynamic models propagate them in the navigation filter.

sections.title: Error sources
sections.text: Orbit errors of kilometres, unknown satellite clocks and atmosphere delays — they must be estimated or differenced away.

sections.title: Orbcomm
sections.text: A LEO messaging constellation whose VHF downlinks give usable Doppler measurements.

sections.title: Starlink
sections.text: Thousands of satellites with high-SNR signals. Doppler can be extracted even without knowing the full signal format.

sections.title: Differential LEO navigation
sections.text: A base station and rover share LEO carrier-phase measurements, cancelling common errors much like RTK.

sections.title: STAN
sections.text: Simultaneous Tracking And Navigation: estimate the LEO satellites' states and your own at the same time.

sections.title: Geometry
sections.text: Even a few LEO satellites give useful DOP because they move so fast across the sky.

sections.title: Simulations
sections.text: Large LEO constellations give metre-level navigation in simulation when GNSS is unavailable.

sections.title: Experiments
sections.text: Real Orbcomm and Starlink tests navigated vehicles and aircraft without GNSS, with errors down to tens of metres.

chapters.title: Inertial Navigation Sensors
chapters.intro: Accelerometers and gyros: navigation without any outside signal.

sections.title: Dead reckoning, perfected
sections.text: Sailors estimated position from speed and heading. An INS does it precisely: integrate acceleration and rotation, with no outside signal needed.

sections.title: Errors grow with time
sections.text: Small sensor errors grow quickly once integrated. Schuler oscillation (84 min) bounds some of them, but position drifts.

sections.title: Performance classes
sections.text: Strategic (~0.1 nmi/h), navigation (~1 nmi/h), tactical and consumer grades — cost and size fall as error grows by orders of magnitude.

sections.title: Accelerometers
sections.text: Most use a proof mass: measure how a spring, pendulum or vibrating beam reacts to specific force. Atom interferometers are the future.

sections.title: Gyroscopes
sections.text: Gyros keep track of heading. Mechanical, ring-laser, fibre-optic and vibrating gyros — navigation grade needs ~0.01°/h stability.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.text: Sixty years of progress made inertial sensors smaller and better — enabling new uses everywhere.

chapters.title: MEMS Inertial Sensors
chapters.intro: The tiny sensors inside every phone.

sections.title: What MEMS is
sections.text: Micro-electro-mechanical systems: mechanical structures microns in size etched from silicon. Tiny, rugged, cheap and low-power.

sections.title: MEMS accelerometers
sections.text: A tiny proof mass on springs. Its movement changes capacitance, which is read out as acceleration.

sections.title: MEMS gyroscopes
sections.text: A vibrating structure feels the Coriolis force when rotated — that tiny sideways motion measures the rotation rate.

sections.title: MEMS IMUs
sections.text: Consumer 3-axis gyros cost ~$0.30. Combined 6- and 9-axis IMUs are in phones, cars and drones.

sections.title: Using them for navigation
sections.text: Great short-term, but biases drift with temperature and time — they need GNSS or other aids, plus calibration.

chapters.title: GNSS-INS Integration
chapters.intro: Combining the best of both: GNSS is stable long-term, INS is smooth short-term.

sections.title: Principles
sections.text: The INS runs continuously, and a Kalman filter estimates its errors from GNSS and subtracts them (error-state filtering).

sections.title: How INS errors grow
sections.text: Attitude errors tilt gravity into false acceleration, biases integrate into drifting velocity and position — models predict this growth.

sections.title: Loose integration
sections.text: Fuse GNSS position/velocity with INS. Simple, but needs a full GNSS fix (4+ satellites).

sections.title: Tight integration
sections.text: Fuse raw pseudoranges and Doppler. Still helpful with only 1–3 satellites in view.

sections.title: Deep integration
sections.text: The INS helps the receiver's tracking loops directly — keeps lock with weaker signals and higher dynamics.

sections.title: Case studies
sections.text: With a MEMS IMU in cities and under dense trees, integration bridges the gaps where GNSS alone fails.

chapters.title: Atomic Clocks for GNSS
chapters.intro: The heart of every navigation satellite.

sections.title: Why clocks matter
sections.text: 1 ns of clock error = 30 cm of range error. GNSS is really a system of very precise flying clocks.

sections.title: How an atomic clock works
sections.text: An oscillator locked to an atomic transition, a counter, and a feedback loop. The atoms keep the frequency honest.

sections.title: Clocks in space
sections.text: Rubidium and caesium standards, and passive hydrogen masers on Galileo. Accuracy and stability are different things.

sections.title: Future space clocks
sections.text: Optical clocks and trapped-ion clocks could be 100× more stable, which would improve orbits and positioning.

sections.title: Relativity
sections.text: Satellite clocks run fast by ~38 µs/day (weaker gravity beats speed). GNSS corrects for it — or positions would drift ~10 km/day.

sections.title: Clocks on the ground
sections.text: Ground control uses even better ensembles of masers and caesium clocks as the master reference.

sections.title: GPS master clock
sections.text: The US Naval Observatory keeps GPS's master clock using a huge array of atomic clocks.

sections.title: Chip-scale atomic clocks
sections.text: DARPA-funded CSACs: a matchbox-size, ~100 mW atomic clock that helps receivers hold time during GNSS outages.

chapters.title: Positioning Using Magnetic Fields
chapters.intro: From compasses to magnetic map matching.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: The compass is ~1000 years old. Today, magnetic anomaly maps allow absolute positioning without GNSS.

sections.title: Sources
sections.text: The core field, crustal anomalies (rocks), and disturbances from the ionosphere, the Sun and your own vehicle all add together.

sections.title: Instruments
sections.text: Fluxgate, optically pumped and other magnetometers. The platform itself (metal, electronics) corrupts measurements.

sections.title: Calibration
sections.text: Aircraft magnetic fields must be modelled and removed (Tolles–Lawson) before the measurements are useful.

sections.title: Magnetic map matching
sections.text: Compare measured anomalies to a map, like terrain matching — demonstrated on flights with errors of tens of metres.

chapters.title: Laser-Based Navigation (Lidar)
chapters.intro: Measuring the world with light.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: Lidar gives precise 3D point clouds used for collision avoidance, mapping and estimating your own motion.

sections.title: Sensor technology
sections.text: Scanning lidars, flash lidars and solid-state units — getting cheaper thanks to self-driving cars.

sections.title: Navigation methods
sections.text: Featureless: align whole point clouds (ICP). Feature-based: extract lines, planes or corners and track them.

sections.title: Considerations
sections.text: SLAM builds the map while navigating. Without loop closure, drift accumulates.

chapters.title: Image-Aided Navigation
chapters.intro: Cameras as navigation sensors.

sections.title: Why cameras
sections.text: Cheap, passive and information-rich. Inspired by how animals navigate by sight.

sections.title: Imaging model
sections.text: An image is a 2D projection of the 3D world. The pinhole camera model links pixels to directions.

sections.title: Interest points
sections.text: Pick features (corners, blobs) that can be found again in the next image.

sections.title: Correspondence
sections.text: Match features between images using descriptors. Wrong matches must be found and rejected.

sections.title: Pose estimation
sections.text: From matched points, solve for camera rotation and translation (e.g. with RANSAC to reject outliers).

sections.title: One camera's limit
sections.text: A single camera can't know scale — it sees motion direction but not distance travelled.

sections.title: Adding information
sections.text: Inertial sensors, known landmarks, stereo or altitude fix the scale and reduce drift.

sections.title: Sensor fusion
sections.text: Camera + IMU (visual-inertial odometry) is now standard in phones, drones and robots.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.text: Image-aided navigation is mature and keeps working where GNSS fails.

chapters.title: Digital Photogrammetry
chapters.intro: Measuring 3D from images.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: Photogrammetry: getting reliable measurements of objects and terrain from images. A long tradition, now merging with navigation.

sections.title: Optical imagery
sections.text: Digital CCD/CMOS cameras replaced film. Sensor quality limits the final product.

sections.title: Basic definitions
sections.text: Spatial, radiometric and spectral resolution; ground sample distance; noise.

sections.title: Fundamentals
sections.text: Collinearity: camera centre, image point and object point lie on one line. Triangulation finds 3D points, backprojection maps them back to images.

sections.title: Workflow
sections.text: Calibrate the camera → orient the images (bundle adjustment, often with GNSS/INS) → dense matching → 3D models and orthophotos.

sections.title: Applications
sections.text: Orthomosaics, digital elevation models, city models, drone mapping, change detection.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.text: Mapping and navigation now feed each other: navigation geo-references images, and images help navigation.

chapters.title: Navigation Using Pulsars and Celestial Sources
chapters.intro: A GPS for deep space.

sections.title: The concept
sections.text: Pulsars are cosmic clocks. Compare pulse arrival times at a spacecraft with predictions at the Solar System's centre → position anywhere in the Solar System.

sections.title: Variable celestial sources
sections.text: Stars guided sailors and Apollo. X-ray pulsars, with their very stable spin, are the best candidates for autonomous space navigation.

sections.title: Applications
sections.text: Deep-space probes, planetary vehicles, even localising gamma-ray bursts. NASA's SEXTANT demonstrated it on the ISS.

sections.title: Limits
sections.text: Faint sources need big detectors and long observation times — today's technology limits accuracy and practicality.

chapters.title: Neuroscience of Navigation
chapters.intro: How the brain knows where you are.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: Navigation is vital for survival. Many animals — and humans — perform remarkable navigation feats.

sections.title: Spatial frameworks
sections.text: Egocentric (relative to me: "left of me") vs allocentric (map-like: "north of the station").

sections.title: Specialised cells
sections.text: Place cells (hippocampus), grid cells, head-direction cells and border cells form the brain's internal GPS — Nobel Prize 2014.

sections.title: Brain systems
sections.text: The hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, parietal cortex and others work together. Damage to them causes getting lost.

sections.title: Future directions
sections.text: How brain areas combine into a full map is still debated. VR and brain imaging are opening new questions.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.text: Since 1978 the field has exploded. It's a rich source of ideas for robot navigation too.

chapters.title: Orientation and Navigation in the Animal World
chapters.intro: Nature's navigation systems.

sections.title: Animal senses
sections.text: Animals use the Sun, stars, smell, polarised light, landmarks and the magnetic field — some senses we don't even have.

sections.title: Star compass
sections.text: Night-migrating songbirds learn the rotation centre of the night sky to find north.

sections.title: Magnetic sense (radical pairs)
sections.text: Light-triggered chemical reactions in the eye (cryptochrome) may let birds "see" the magnetic field.

sections.title: Other mechanisms
sections.text: Tiny magnetite crystals might act as internal compass needles. How animals combine all these cues remains a big open question.

chapters.title: Surveying and Mobile Mapping
chapters.intro: GNSS for measuring land and building maps.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: Multi-GNSS and augmentation made centimetre positioning routine for surveyors.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.text: Accuracy needs vary: cadastral boundaries need centimetres, GIS mapping can accept decimetres to metres.

sections.title: Land and marine surveying
sections.text: RTK and network RTK for land, and DGNSS/PPP via satellite links for offshore and hydrographic surveys.

sections.title: Mobile mapping
sections.text: Cars, drones and backpacks with GNSS/INS + lidar + cameras map roads and cities quickly.

sections.title: Emerging trends
sections.text: Multi-frequency, cheap high-precision receivers, PPP-RTK and smartphone raw measurements are changing surveying.

chapters.title: Precision Agriculture
chapters.intro: GNSS on the farm.

sections.title: What it is
sections.text: GIS maps plus GNSS guidance: auto-steering tractors, variable-rate seeding and spraying, yield maps.

sections.title: GNSS requirements
sections.text: Repeatable centimetre accuracy (come back next season to the same row), ionospheric scintillation near the equator, and correction services.

sections.title: Plate motion matters
sections.text: Continents move cm per year, so field coordinates drift against global frames — correction services must handle the datum.

chapters.title: Wearables
chapters.intro: Navigation and sensing on your body.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: Wearables were science fiction for a century — now they're on everyone's wrist.

sections.title: Origins
sections.text: GPS in consumer devices after Selective Availability ended in 2000 opened the door to running watches and trackers.

sections.title: The wearable world
sections.text: Fitness bands, smartwatches, hearables, smart glasses and clothing — a crowded market.

sections.title: Architecture
sections.text: Wearable gathers data → phone processes and connects → cloud stores and analyses.

sections.title: Sensors
sections.text: GNSS, MEMS motion sensors, barometers, heart-rate and other biosensors.

sections.title: Battery is king
sections.text: Power is the biggest design constraint. GNSS duty-cycling and low-power chips extend battery life.

sections.title: Video and audio
sections.text: Cameras and audio add features but drain batteries — always a trade-off.

sections.title: Wireless
sections.text: Bluetooth Low Energy dominates. Wi-Fi and cellular are used sparingly because of power.

sections.title: Privacy & security
sections.text: Location and health data are sensitive — studies found wearables leaking them.

sections.title: The future
sections.text: Networked body sensors giving a holistic picture of health and performance.

sections.title: Summary
sections.text: Wearables will become everywhere and nearly invisible — woven into daily life.

chapters.title: Navigation for ADAS and Automated Driving
chapters.intro: How self-driving cars know where they are.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: ~37,000 road deaths a year in the US and over a million worldwide. Automation promises safety — and it needs precise, reliable positioning.

sections.title: Useful GNSS measurements
sections.text: Besides position: velocity, heading (course), road grade and time-differenced carrier phase for precise motion.

sections.title: Vehicle models
sections.text: Combining GNSS with vehicle dynamics models and IMUs estimates slip, heading and tyre behaviour.

sections.title: Applications
sections.text: Lane-level navigation, vehicle state estimation, and guidance and control — e.g. estimating tyre-road friction.

chapters.title: Train Control and Rail Traffic Management
chapters.intro: GNSS on the railway.

sections.title: The role of GNSS
sections.text: Knowing train position precisely lets trains run closer together safely. GNSS could replace expensive track-side balises.

sections.title: Track-constrained PNT
sections.text: Trains stay on tracks, so the problem becomes 1D along a known track map — a big help.

sections.title: GNSS + odometer
sections.text: Wheel odometers bridge tunnels and GNSS gaps, while GNSS corrects odometer slip.

sections.title: Relative positioning
sections.text: Differential positioning against reference stations, constrained to the track geometry, gives high accuracy.

sections.title: Which track am I on?
sections.text: Parallel tracks are only a few metres apart, so track discrimination needs carrier phase and integrity.

sections.title: Detector performance
sections.text: Multipath near stations and integrity requirements set how reliably the right track is identified.

chapters.title: Commercial Unmanned Aircraft (UAS)
chapters.intro: Navigation for drones.

sections.title: Context
sections.text: Commercial drone uses are booming — delivery, inspection, mapping — while the military remains the biggest operator.

sections.title: Guidance and autonomy
sections.text: A strategic layer plans the route, a tactical layer reacts in real time. Navigation feeds both.

sections.title: Avoiding terrain and obstacles
sections.text: Path planning with sensors and maps keeps drones away from buildings, terrain and wires.

sections.title: Avoiding other aircraft
sections.text: Detect-and-avoid systems issue warnings and manoeuvres to keep safe separation.

sections.title: Role of navigation
sections.text: Navigation errors must be accounted for in safety zones — integrity matters for drones too.

chapters.title: Navigation for Aviation
chapters.intro: Past, present and future of finding your way in the sky.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: Airspace is modernising: more and different aircraft, more efficient routes — all built on precision navigation.

sections.title: History
sections.text: From landmarks and beacons to radio ranges, VOR/DME, ILS and INS — each era added new tools.

sections.title: The 21st century
sections.text: GNSS is primary, terrestrial radio is the backup, and new signals (cellular, LEO) serve drones.

sections.title: GNSS in aviation
sections.text: RAIM, SBAS and GBAS are certified for all flight phases — from oceanic routes to landing.

sections.title: Terrestrial backups
sections.text: NDB, VOR and DME remain as a safety net if GNSS fails — DME networks are getting renewed attention.

sections.title: Surveillance-based navigation
sections.text: Radar and ADS-B tracking can also help aircraft know where they are.

sections.title: Signals of opportunity
sections.text: Urban drone delivery needs metre-level navigation in places aviation never used — cellular and other signals may help.

sections.title: Natural sources
sections.text: Inertial, barometric, magnetic and terrain-based navigation fill gaps, especially for drones.

sections.title: Vision
sections.text: Enhanced and synthetic vision let pilots "see" through fog and darkness, and cameras increasingly navigate drones.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.text: More users, more variety, new vehicles like suborbital spaceflight — aviation navigation must become multi-source.

chapters.title: Orbit Determination with GNSS
chapters.intro: GNSS receivers in space tracking satellites.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: Almost every LEO satellite carries a GPS receiver — the most efficient and accurate way to track spacecraft.

sections.title: Formulation
sections.text: Positioning a satellite with GNSS is like positioning a user on the ground — but it's moving at 7 km/s.

sections.title: Linearisation
sections.text: Orbit models (gravity, drag, solar pressure) are linearised around an initial guess and refined iteratively.

sections.title: Kinematic, dynamic, reduced-dynamic
sections.text: Kinematic: GNSS only. Dynamic: physics model only. Reduced-dynamic: both — the best of each.

sections.title: The reference matters
sections.text: Precise GNSS orbits and clocks (from IGS/JPL) are the reference — their quality limits yours.

sections.title: Validation
sections.text: Check against laser ranging (SLR) and orbit overlaps to know how good the solution really is.

sections.title: LEO, MEO, HEO
sections.text: Higher orbits see GNSS signals only from the far side of Earth — weak, sparse, but still usable even at GEO.

sections.title: Formation flying
sections.text: Differential GNSS between spacecraft gives millimetre-to-centimetre relative positions.

sections.title: Space receivers
sections.text: Radiation hardening, export controls (above 18 km / 515 m/s) and high dynamics set space receivers apart.

sections.title: Timing
sections.text: Receiver clock states can tie onboard instruments precisely to a known time scale.

sections.title: Earth science POD
sections.text: Altimetry and gravity missions need cm- to mm-level orbits — GNSS made that possible.

sections.title: Combining data
sections.text: SLR, DORIS, star trackers and accelerometers combine with GNSS for the best orbits.

sections.title: Onboard orbit determination
sections.text: Real-time orbits computed on the satellite itself, with limited computing — getting closer to ground quality.

sections.title: Jason-3 case study
sections.text: An ocean-altimetry satellite whose cm-level orbits rely on GNSS together with DORIS and SLR.

chapters.title: Satellite Formation Flying and Rendezvous
chapters.intro: Spacecraft flying in tight formation.

sections.title: Relative navigation
sections.text: GNSS measurements give the relative positions of cooperating satellites — key for formations and docking.

sections.title: Relative orbit determination
sections.text: Estimate how satellites move relative to each other. Carrier-phase differencing gives mm–cm precision.

sections.title: Mission results
sections.text: Space Shuttle, PRISMA, TanDEM-X and NASA's MMS (using GPS far above the GNSS constellation!) all proved it.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.text: Accurate relative navigation enables precise formation control — the basis for distributed space systems.

chapters.title: Navigation in the Arctic
chapters.intro: The hardest place on Earth to navigate.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: Melting sea ice is opening Arctic shipping routes — but navigation there is extremely difficult.

sections.title: Ice navigation
sections.text: Poor charts, moving ice, extreme cold and darkness. Ships rely on GNSS, radar, ice charts and experience.

sections.title: GNSS integrity in the Arctic
sections.text: Satellites sit low on the horizon, the ionosphere is stormy, and SBAS coverage is thin. Multi-GNSS and new infrastructure help.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.text: Harsh conditions make the Arctic one of the most hostile places to navigate — and a growing priority.
